variants.name: Strict bilateral symmetry about a central entrance
variants.note: The style's identity. Every elevation is composed; the rear and the ends are elevations too, not leftovers.
The normative front.
Smaller houses and urban lots.
The largest houses.
Main block, hyphens, dependencies. Symmetry extended to the whole complex rather than abandoned.
The only permitted accent, 12-36 in, and it must be on the centre bay.
There is no centre to enter. This is the style's one hard proportional constraint and until 0.2.0 there was no slot to state it in.

THE SLOT-LEVEL PROHIBITION THAT WAS UNSAYABLE IN 0.1.0. A Georgian house composed picturesquely is not a Georgian house with a defect; it is a different species. The regularity is a claim about the owner's mind.
Near-symmetry with a deliberate offset is Queen Anne Free Classic and Shingle Style. Georgian symmetry is arithmetic, not visual balance.
Growth by accretion. What the style replaced — and note that telescoping in the Chesapeake is accretion tolerated behind a composed front, not in it.
Except in the side-hall urban variant, where the THREE-BAY front is itself composed about the door of a narrower parti.

centre_bay_treatment.note: Never by a projecting mass, except on the most ambitious Palladian compositions.

pavilion_projection.note: The only permitted break in the front plane, and only on the centre bay.

elevations_composed.note: Trim consistency on all four elevations is a REVIVAL tell; composition on all four is a Georgian one. The distinction is that the rear is composed to a lower rank, not to the same rank.

composition_parti.rule: The front elevation is strictly bilaterally symmetrical about a central entrance in an odd number of bays — three, five or seven — with the centre distinguished only by the doorway; a picturesque or balanced-asymmetrical parti is forbidden outright.

packs.note: The pack enforces odd parity arithmetically, which is the whole reason to bind it.

composition_parti.note: THE SLOT I ASKED FOR AND THE MOST IMPORTANT ONE IN THE FILE. In 0.1.0 the defining fact about this style lived in proportional_system.symmetry on the taxonomy record, which does not cascade and is not a kit slot, and the three prohibitions above could not be written anywhere at all. Everything in the kit that reads as a rule about rhythm — window_grouping_rule, wing_strategy, gable_treatment, roof_form's ban on picturesque intersections — is downstream of this slot and was previously orphaned.

variants.note: Regionally restricted. Effectively absent in the Chesapeake and the Low Country.
Breaks the single unaccented cornice line the whole composition depends on. Victorian.
Turns the gable into the principal elevation, which inverts the style's parti.
First Period. An asymmetrical section under a symmetrical front is a contradiction.
Second Empire, and 120 years late.
No period existence on a main block.
Two roofs of unequal ridge height meeting on the main block. This is the roof-scale form of the asymmetrical parti now forbidden at composition_parti.

hip_ridge_length_ratio.note: Ridge length as a fraction of the building length on a hipped roof. Below a quarter the roof reads pyramidal; above a half the hips read as clipped gables.

roof_form.rule: The roof is one simple solid about one ridge, of equal pitch on all slopes, unbroken across the full length of the main block; the only permitted interruptions are chimneys and dormers set in the bay rhythm.
roof_form.note: FORBIDDEN VARIANTS, recorded here because the schema has nowhere else to put them: cross-gable, front-gable, catslide/saltbox (that is First Period), mansard (Second Empire), shed, and any picturesque intersection of two roofs of unequal ridge height on the main block. This is the first place the ontology bit: a slot can be 'specified' or 'forbidden' but cannot be 'specified with these variants forbidden', and for a style whose identity is largely a set of prohibitions that loses most of the information. Gambrel is regionally restricted — common in New England and the Hudson Valley, effectively absent in the Chesapeake.

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country

roof_pitch.rule: Rise:run between 8:12 and 10:12 on the main block, and identical on every slope; a wing or dependency may not differ by more than 1:12 from the main block.
roof_pitch.note: One of the two highest-signal numbers in the whole kit. Below 7:12 the cornice loses its relation to the roof and the house reads Federal or later; above 11:12 it reads First Period. The regional band inside this range is a real climate gradient and it runs north-steep to south-shallow, which is snow load and nothing else. Converted to `extends` to test three-level inheritance: what English Georgian already establishes is no longer restated here (2 field(s) removed).
roof_pitch.rule_append: Colonial roofs run a course steeper than the English norm and are never concealed behind a parapet.

variants.note: Urban and masonry work. A slate roof on a clapboard farmhouse is a status claim the rest of the building does not support.
Plain three-tab only, and an acknowledged modern substitution rather than a correct answer. Listed because pretending otherwise makes the kit unusable.
Spanish and Mediterranean. No Anglo-colonial existence.
Rolled sheet metal roofing is a nineteenth-century product. Correct on a Greek Revival house, wrong here.
Wrong twice over: it is not a period material and it fakes a shadow the real material does not cast.
A shake is split thick and irregular; a colonial shingle is dressed with a draw-knife to a taper. The difference reads from the street.

shingle_length.note: Historic range across all periods is 14-36 in; 18-24 in is the colonial norm.

shingle_exposure.note: Not more than one third of the shingle length.

shingle_width.note: Width limited to under 10 in to prevent curling.

roof_material.rule: Wood shingle laid at not more than one third of its length to the weather; slate only where the house is masonry and urban; standing-seam metal, barrel tile and dimensional 'architectural' composition shingle are all wrong and the last is wrong twice over, because it fakes a shadow the real material does not cast.
sources: NPS Preservation Brief 19: The Repair and Replacement of Historic Wooden Shingle Roofs
roof_material.note: Shingle figures from NPS Preservation Brief 19, which gives historic lengths of 14-36 in, widths of 3-8 in, butts of 3/8-3/4 in, and the one-third exposure rule. Composition shingle is listed as a permitted variant only in its plain three-tab form and only as an acknowledged modern substitution; it is in the list because pretending otherwise makes the kit unusable, not because it is correct.

variants.note: The single most common failure of a modern Georgian. The wall must terminate in an entablature, not in the structure that holds the roof up.
Italianate. A bracket is a substitute for an order, not a member of one.
The soffit is level because the corona is level. A sloping soffit is a rafter-tail eave with a board over it.
An eave whose depth is set by the gutter rather than by the order. See the rainwater slot for where the gutter actually goes.

cornice_height_in.note: the cornice member of the Gibbs Ionic entablature, taken at the storey

entablature_height_in.note: Gibbs makes the entablature one FIFTH of the column; Vignola makes it one quarter

cornice_projection_in.note: projection past the wall face at a 9 ft bay

soffit.value: closed, plastered or boarded, level (not raked)

eave_condition.rule: The eave is a classical entablature, not a trim board: the wall terminates in architrave, frieze and cornice derived from the bound order, boxed, with a level closed soffit and the corona projecting far enough to cast a shadow across the frieze.

packs.note: The order governs the eave on a frame house.
On a masonry house a corbelled cornice is physically a whole number of courses and the brick gauge wins.

eave_condition.note: FORBIDDEN, and with no way to say so in the schema: exposed rafter tails, a bracketed or bracket-supported eave, a raked (sloping) soffit, a fascia-and-gutter eave with no frieze, and any eave whose projection is set by the gutter rather than by the order. The exposed rafter tail is the single most common failure of a modern Georgian and it is invisible to a slot model that only records what a style HAS.

rake_overhang_in.note: OQ 19: not an independent claim. `rake_to_cornice_ratio` beside it, 0.5 to 0.7, IS the derivation from the `cornice` slot this record names as its determiner; this range is the band that ratio lands in on a Georgian eave, kept because a builder reads inches and an engine reads the ratio. Where the two disagree the ratio governs, because it is the one that moves with the cornice.

rake_to_cornice_ratio.note: The raking member is a REDUCED eave cornice — bed mould and crown without corona and modillions. The reduction ratio is my convention expressed as a band; what is documented is only that the verge is tight relative to the eave.

rake_condition.rule: The rake is tight — 4 to 8 in of overhang — and carries a reduced version of the eave profile; it must die into the cornice return rather than meeting it in a mitre.
rake_condition.note: The rake-to-cornice reduction ratio is a judgment call expressed as a band rather than a documented figure. What is documented is the tightness of the verge relative to the eave, which is universal in surviving colonial work.

variants.note: A twentieth-century economy and the fastest way to date a Georgian-looking house to after 1930.

cornice_return.rule: The cornice returns across the full depth of the gable end carrying its complete profile, including the modillion or dentil band, for 12 to 24 in before dying into the wall.
cornice_return.note: FORBIDDEN: the clipped triangular 'pork chop' return, which is a twentieth-century economy and is the fastest way to date a Georgian-looking house to after 1930. The 12-24 in figure is from the new-england-georgian node and is the best-documented of the regional variants; the Southern brick houses often return the cornice all the way round instead, which is a different and also correct answer.

variants.note: Urban party-wall condition only. A fire wall, not a compositional choice.
Medieval survival or Tudor Revival. Not colonial Georgian.
Shingle Style and Queen Anne.
Carpenter Gothic.
English vernacular and Tudor Revival.
Any sunburst, fan, louvre panel or applied trim in the field of the gable.

pediment_rise_in.note: rise over the span of the pavilion or portico it crowns; at a 45 ft span

pediment_rise_ratio.value: 1 : 5 of the span (facade-classical); Palladian practice runs 1:4.5 to 1:5.5

gable_treatment.rule: The gable end is a plain wall terminated by the cornice return; a pediment appears only where a centre pavilion or a portico breaks forward, and its rise is one fifth of its span.
gable_treatment.note: FORBIDDEN: half-timbering, shingled gables, bargeboards, jerkinheads, and applied gable ornament of any kind. The parapeted brick end is included as a permitted variant only for urban party-wall conditions in Charleston and Philadelphia, where it is a fire wall and not a compositional choice.

variants.note: No period existence on a principal elevation; a twentieth-century attic conversion.
Shingle Style and Richardsonian.
Breaks the eave line, which no Georgian dormer does.

dormer_window_height_in.note: the dormer follows the ATTIC storey (0.62) rather than the storey below it

alignment_rule.value: each dormer centred on a window of the storey below

cheek_width.note: Practical band from surviving work rather than a documented rule.

sash_pattern.note: One storey-step smaller than the second-floor sash.

dormer.rule: Dormers align exactly on the bays below, are odd in number, carry the same order as the house at reduced scale, and never break the eave line.
dormer.note: Dormers are common on gabled Georgian houses and on Chesapeake hipped roofs, rarer on the grandest hipped town houses where the attic is lit from the ends. The cheek width band is a practical figure from surviving work rather than a documented rule.

variants.name: Paired stacks joined above the roof by an arched brick curtain

variants.note: The First Period signature and the thing the Georgian plan was invented to replace. Read the chimney and the roof pitch, not the trim.

stack_plan_in.note: chimney plan dimensions are whole bricks; a stack is 1.5 x 2 bricks (13.5 x 18 in), 2 x 2 (18 in), 2 x 3 (18 x 27 in)

cap_courses.note: Corbelled brick cap, or a moulded stone cap.

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country

chimney.rule: Chimneys are paired and symmetrically disposed — never a single central stack, which is the First Period signature — and their plan dimensions are whole bricks.
chimney.note: Position is the single fastest regional discriminator in the style and it is a plan decision, not a roof decision: New England sets them inboard of the ridge to keep the stored heat inside; the Chesapeake and Low Country put them at the gable ends, often fully exterior, to keep the heat out. The same slot therefore carries opposite climate logic in two children, which is exactly what the cascade is for.

permitted_on_rear_slope.note: The historical half of this list is the first two.

roof_penetration_rules.rule: Nothing penetrates the entrance slope of the roof except a chimney or a dormer set in the bay rhythm; every modern penetration — plumbing vent, flue, fan, array — goes on the rear slope, below the ridge line and out of the approach cone.
roof_penetration_rules.note: JUDGMENT AND PARTLY INVENTION. The historical rule is simply that only chimneys and dormers existed. The modern half — vents and arrays to the rear, painted out, capped at 12 in — is authored here, on the same principle that governs the historical half: the entrance elevation and its roof are a composition and nothing uncomposed may appear on them. It is a weaker piece of invention than garage_strategy because it has an obvious right answer.

second_over_first.note: second storey over first, storey to storey

attic_over_second.note: attic or half-storey over the floor below

window_height_second_over_first.value: 0.82 to 0.88 measured (style node); 5/6 = 0.833 by Palladio's rule, compounding by storey

front_height_over_width.note: the composed front is 2.5 bays high; at a 45 ft five-bay front this is 0.5

height_proportion.rule: Each storey is 0.85 of the one below it, storey to storey, and the window heights follow at 0.82-0.88; the graduation is what makes the front sit on the ground instead of floating.

packs.note: A different quantity — the whole front's height over its width, not the storey ratio. Kept because they are routinely confused.

height_proportion.note: The measured band (0.82-0.88) and Palladio's rule (5/6 = 0.833) agree to within two per cent, which is the reason to trust either. The first casualty of a modern equal-height frame is this slot, and its loss is invisible in plan and fatal in elevation.

variants.note: A five-bay box with no wing at all is entirely correct and is the commonest form.

wing_ridge_rule.note: A wing whose ridge equals the main block's is a second house.

wing_strategy.rule: A wing is subordinate in every dimension — lower ridge, shallower depth, set back from the main facade plane — and where wings are symmetrical they must be identical, because a five-part composition with unequal dependencies is not a composition.
wing_strategy.note: The five-part Palladian composition is the ambition of the plantation and the great town seat; the subordinate ell is the ordinary answer. Note that 'telescoping' is a Chesapeake growth pattern rather than a designed composition, and that the two answer different questions — one is how the house is designed, the other is how it grew.

variants.note: Oak or mixed hardwood box frame, mortise and tenon, with the 16 ft bay of the timber-bay pack still setting the depth.

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country

variants.note: 13.5 in of brick with a real through-bond. This is what makes Flemish bond possible.
18 in, on the largest houses and on stone work.

THE SLOT THAT DID NOT EXIST. A single 3 5/8 in wythe cannot be laid in Flemish or English bond, because both are through-bonds defined by headers passing into the wall's depth: a 'Flemish bond' veneer is half-bricks glued to a backup and the giveaway is that the header and the stretcher have the same face. It also collapses the reveal from 4-8 in to nothing and leaves the water table and belt course with no wall-thickness change to weather. Three separate slots in this kit are unbuildable on a veneer and until 0.2.0 nothing recorded why.
1830s. A Georgian house cannot be balloon-framed and remain a colonial one, though a Georgian Revival house obviously can.
The honest modern substitution for the frame variants, and the one that must then re-derive the reveal by furring or by a deeper jamb.
Defensible only if the reveal and the cornice bearing are solved explicitly; the panel gives neither for free.

masonry_wall_thickness.note: The thickness at which Flemish and English bond are even available.

wythe_step_at_floor.note: SUSPECT, flagged 24 Aug 2026 (OQ 19) and deliberately not changed: this reads 13.5 in, which is `masonry_wall_thickness` above it repeated verbatim, and a step at a floor line cannot be the whole thickness of the wall. `reveal_masonry.step_at_floor_in` says 4.5 in, a half brick, and its rule sentence says a half brick. Correcting a number on a guess is worse than recording that two slots disagree, so this is recorded. Whoever has the source decides.

construction_type.rule: The wall is structural: solid masonry of not less than two wythes with a real through-bond, or a braced timber frame; a masonry veneer over a frame is forbidden because it makes the bond, the reveal and the water table all fictions.
construction_type.note: This slot is the discriminator that half the envelope and opening group now depends on: primary_cladding, wall_thickness_expression, window_head, window_surround and cornice all carry applies_when.construction values that were previously prose. It is also the slot most likely to be argued with by a builder, and that argument is now about one field instead of five.

variants.note: Boarding scored and sanded to imitate ashlar, with sand in the paint. A wooden wall imitating stone is a New England high-style tell.

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country

variants.note: Carpenter Gothic. Vertical boarding has no colonial Georgian existence.
Wall shingles are correct on a First Period or Shingle Style house and wrong on a Georgian front, where the wall wants a horizontal course line.
Not a period-material objection so much as a profile one: neither holds the 3/4 in butt thickness or the 1/8 in bed a riven clapboard casts its shadow off.

brick_course_in.note: one course: a 2 1/4 in brick with a 1/2 in bed joint

brick_four_courses_in.note: four courses to eleven inches — the mason's gauge

clapboard_exposure.source: ICAA, Classical Comments: Weatherboards and Clapboards

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country

weatherboard_exposure.note: Sawn pine or poplar, about 8 in wide, lapped 1.5 in. Cypress in South Carolina.

bond_entrance_elevation.value: Flemish, with glazed headers in the Chesapeake

primary_cladding.rule: One cladding per volume, laid to a real module — the board exposure or the brick gauge — and carried identically round all four elevations of that volume.
sources: Institute of Classical Architecture & Art, Classical Comments: Weatherboards and Clapboards
primary_cladding.note: Northern clapboard and Southern weatherboard are different products and the numbers are not interchangeable: riven oak clapboards 40-48 in long at 3.25-4.25 in to the weather in New England, sawn pine or poplar weatherboards about 8 in wide at 6 in to the weather with a 1.5 in lap in the Mid-Atlantic and South (ICAA, Classical Comments: Weatherboards and Clapboards). A Virginia house sided at 4 in exposure looks Northern and a Massachusetts house at 6 in looks wrong in a way most people cannot name.

secondary_cladding.rule: A single volume has one cladding material, top to bottom and on all four elevations; there is no second material.
secondary_cladding.note: This is a genuine slot-level 'forbidden' and one of only two in this kit. It is the rule that kills the brick-front-with-vinyl-returns pathology at the root rather than patching it at material_change_rule. A dependency, a hyphen or a later ell may be clad differently — but those are different VOLUMES, and the distinction between a volume and an elevation is the whole content of the rule. Note the schema cannot express 'forbidden within a volume, permitted between volumes', so the qualification lives in prose here.

min_belt_projection_in.note: the minimum projection at which a horizontal reads as a real change of wall thickness

set: a change of volume (main block to hyphen, hyphen to dependency, main block to ell)
below the water table, where the foundation may be stone under a brick or frame wall

material_change_rule.rule: Material may change only where the building changes volume or where a projecting horizontal course runs the full way round; it may never change at an unreturned corner, never at a storey line that is not expressed by a real projection, and never on the entrance elevation alone.
material_change_rule.note: The one rule in this kit that is written against a modern failure mode rather than from period fabric. Its period justification is real, though: in a load-bearing wall the material changed where the wall thickness changed, and the water table and belt course exist to weather that step. Where the wall is a veneer over a frame there is no step and the courses become foam-backed bumps — see brick-course's own conflict note on continuous exterior insulation.

exposed_height_in.note: exposed foundation below the water table at a 9 ft bay

exposed_height_alt_in.note: the same dimension taken from the storey instead of the bay

foundation_expression.rule: The foundation shows for 18 to 24 in below the water table, in a material and bond coarser than the wall above, and it is the same height all the way round the volume even where the grade falls.

packs.note: 18 in from the bay, 24 in from the storey. Both inside the measured band; the facade pack wins because the foundation is read in elevation.

foundation_expression.note: Two bound packs give 18 in and 24 in for the same dimension from different modules. Both are inside the measured band and neither is wrong; there is no rule in the schema for choosing between them, which is a real finding rather than a defect in either pack.

variants.note: A Georgian house is never without a water table. A brick wall that starts at grade has no plinth and the house appears dropped rather than built.

height_above_grade_in.note: ten courses — the canonical masonry answer

height_alt_in.note: the same datum taken from the bay

projection_in.note: about two inches — one course set out

water_table.rule: A moulded or bevelled water table runs 24 to 36 in above finished grade — ten brick courses where the wall is brick — projects about 2 in, and returns fully round every elevation of the volume including the rear.

packs.note: Ten courses. In masonry this is not negotiable — it must land on a course.

water_table.note: This is the datum the whole elevation is measured up from and the one horizontal a Georgian house is never without. It is also the cheapest thing to omit and the omission is instantly legible: a brick wall that starts at grade has no plinth and the house appears to have been dropped rather than built.

variants.note: Rare on New England frame houses, where there is no wall-thickness change to express. Effectively mandatory in the Mid-Atlantic.

band_depth_in.note: two courses: a moulded or bevelled brick over a plain projecting course

band_depth_alt_in.note: the same band taken from the bay module

projection_in.note: one course set out, or a 5/4 board

height_above_first_floor_in.note: the belt sits at the second-floor STRUCTURE, about 6 in above the top of the first storey

belt_course.rule: Where a belt course occurs it sits at the second-floor structure, not at the second-floor finish, runs the full width of every elevation, and projects about 2 in.

packs.note: Gives the HEIGHT of the band above the floor, not its depth. Different quantity, same slot.

belt_course.note: Regionally conditional and that is the interesting part: canonical and effectively non-negotiable in the Mid-Atlantic, optional in the Chesapeake, rare on New England frame houses where there is no wall-thickness change to express. 'none' is a real permitted variant here, which is a different statement from binding the slot open.

variants.note: Rubbed brick or nothing at all is the canonical Tidewater answer.

quoin_course_height_in.note: quoins must alternate on a whole number of courses or the corner will not close

pack_derived_width_in.note: what the facade pack gives for the corner at a 9 ft bay

corner_quoin.rule: The corner is expressed by a member of the bound order — a board, a pilaster or a quoin — whose width is constant for the full height of the volume, and quoins alternate on a whole number of courses.

packs.note: Quoins alternate on a whole number of courses or the corner will not close.

reveal_in.note: Renamed from `reveal_masonry` and its `applies_when.construction` dropped: a parameter named after its own slot, discriminated on the condition the slot already IS, was the duplication saying so twice.

reveal_masonry.rule: The reveal at every masonry opening expresses the real thickness of the wall -- 4 to 8 in -- and the wall steps in by a half brick at each floor level, not continuously.
reveal_masonry.note: OQ 19, 24 Aug 2026, second pass. OQ 19, 24 Aug 2026. parapet.rule: The wall terminates in the cornice and the roof is shown; there is no parapet concealing it.

An ogee-profile aluminium gutter reads as a second, wrong crown moulding stuck on the front of a correct one. It is the single most common way a well-detailed cornice is ruined after the fact.
A downpipe in the approach cone. Take the water round the corner in the cornice or accept the drip.
An eave whose projection is set by the gutter rather than by the order. Recorded at eave_condition too, because the failure happens at both ends.

leader_position.value: at the corners of the volume, never on the entrance elevation

grade_fall_min.note: 6 in in the first 10 ft, which is also the IRC's own figure and agrees with the period practice of falling grade away from a water table.

cornice_projection_min_for_no_gutter.note: Below about 8 in of projection the drip line lands on the wall and the no-gutter answer stops working.

rainwater.note: Half retrieved and half authored. window_lite_pattern.note: This slot is the one that most rewards being told the date. The style's one genuinely hard proportional constraint, now also stated at composition_parti: an even-bay Georgian front has no centre to enter.

pier_width_in.note: the wall between windows at a 9 ft bay

vertical_alignment.value: upper-storey windows centred exactly on the openings below

window_grouping_rule.rule: Windows appear as singles, evenly spaced, in an odd number of bays with the entrance in the centre bay; upper windows align exactly over lower ones; there are no pairs, no ribbons and no blank bays on the entrance elevation.
window_grouping_rule.note: The odd-bay rule is the style's one genuinely hard proportional constraint and it is the rule that makes the entrance possible: an even-bay Georgian front has no centre to enter. Blank bays are permitted on gable ends where a chimney occupies the wall, and were sometimes built as blind windows with painted sash — a period solution that is worth having and that nothing in the ontology can express.

leaf_width_in.note: half the opening less the meeting clearance, so the closed pair actually covers the window

leaf_height.value: equal to the full sash height

hardware.value: strap or pintle hinges, and a holdback (shutter dog) at each leaf

louver_date.value: louvered shutters are a Southern device and appear from the mid eighteenth century; panelled is the earlier and Northern answer

shutter.rule: Shutter leaves are half the clear opening width less the meeting clearance and the full height of the sash, hung on real pintles with real holdbacks, so that a closed pair exactly covers the window.
shutter.note: Half-width shutters are named in the style node as the single commonest tell of a fake traditional facade, and the arithmetic is not subtle: a 36 in window needs a 17.5 in leaf and gets a 12 in one from a catalogue. If a house cannot afford correct shutters it should have none — a Georgian house without shutters is austere and a Georgian house with decorative ones is a lie.

venetian_from_sidelight_in.note: total width run forward from the side-light width; run it BACKWARDS from the bay in practice

placement.value: centre bay of the second storey, over the entrance, or in a pediment

width_from_storey_in.note: the rule to run FIRST, before any door is chosen

panel_arrangement.value: six panels: two short over two tall over two short, raised and fielded on the outer face
