garage_strategy.rule: The car is housed in a subordinate volume that obeys the dependency rules the style already has — set back not less than 20 ft behind the front plane, at 0.6 to 0.75 of the main block height, with its doors turned off the entrance elevation and never wider than 9 ft each.
garage_strategy.note: INVENTION, AND MARKED AS SUCH. There is no precedent for this slot and none can be found: Georgian America had no cars, and the carriage house it did have was a farm building at the back of the lot, not an attached room off the kitchen. What is retrieved rather than invented is the RULE SET this answer is built out of, which is the style's own: the five-part composition already knows how to subordinate a service volume — hyphen 12-20 ft, dependency at 60-75 per cent of the main block's height, detached service not less than 25 ft away — and a garage is a service volume. So the invention is the identification of the car with the kitchen dependency, and everything downstream of that follows from rules the style genuinely has. THE PART THAT IS PURE ASSERTION and cannot be defended from any source: the 20 ft setback, the 9 ft door width, and the refusal of a single wide door. I chose them because a 16 ft door has no proportional relative anywhere in the kit — there is no other 16 ft opening in a Georgian house — while a 9 ft door is close enough to the 0.8-of-a-bay entrance cap to sit in the same family. That is an argument from consistency, not from evidence, and a reviewer is entitled to disagree with it. WHAT I WOULD DEFEND HARDEST: that the garage may not face the street on the entrance elevation, at any width, for any client. Everything else here is negotiable.

variants.note: Crown or cylinder glass, 7/8 in muntin, 1 3/8 in sash. The historical assembly and the one every dimension in window_type is derived from.

THE AUTHORED ANSWER. A removable or fixed interior storm panel behind a true single-glazed sash gets to about U-0.35 while leaving the muntin, the sash depth, the reveal and the reflection untouched. It is reversible, it is what the conservation literature recommends, and it is invisible from the street.

Insulated glass in a true divided sash forces the muntin to about 1 1/8-1 1/4 in and the sash to 1 3/4 in or more. Defensible where a storm panel is impossible, and it should be acknowledged that the window has thickened.
An applied grille with a shadow bar between the panes. The giveaway is that the grille and the glass are in different planes and the reflection runs continuously behind the muntin.
Worse: a plastic lattice clipped to a single sheet.
Worst: a muntin that casts no shadow at all and cannot be painted.
A triple-track aluminium storm reads as a second window in front of the first and flattens the reveal the masonry variants exist to express.

muntin_width_insulated_min.note: What a true divided insulated unit actually forces. The number is the argument.

interior_storm_u_factor.note: Approximate assembly U-factor for a single-glazed sash with a well-fitted interior panel. Cited as an order of magnitude, not a rating.

glazing_assembly.rule: The sash is single-glazed with true divided lights and a 7/8 in muntin; where thermal performance is required it is met with an interior storm panel behind the historic sash, never by thickening the muntin or by simulating it.

code_conflict.code_requirement: U-0.30 to U-0.32 maximum fenestration U-factor in climate zones 4-6
code_conflict.resolution: Historic replacement windows are commonly exempt, but a new-build traditional house is not. The interior storm panel is the assembly that comes closest while leaving every visible dimension intact; where it cannot reach code, take the exception on the principal elevation and use insulated true-divided units on the rear, which is a documented and legible hierarchy rather than a uniform compromise.

glazing_assembly.note: Exactly the trade-off I said had nowhere to live. Note what the slot makes visible that prose could not: the muntin goes from 7/8 in to 1 1/4 in — a 43 per cent increase in the single most diagnostic dimension on the building — and that is the actual price of insulated glass, stated as a number instead of as a worry.

variants.note: The richest interiors and a handful of porticos only.
The Greek orders arrive with Benjamin's 1830 plates. A baseless Greek Doric on a colonial house is a fifty-year anachronism.
The baseless Greek Ionic arrives with Asher Benjamin's 1830 plates, a hundred years after this style begins. Same anachronism as the Greek Doric.
The whole point of the style is that the order is drawn from a book to a rule. An abstracted order is what the style replaced.

entablature_over_column.note: Gibbs: one fifth. Vignola: one quarter. At a 10 in diameter that is 18 in against 22.5 in

authority.value: Gibbs, Rules for Drawing the Several Parts of Architecture (1732)
authority.source: Helen Park, A List of Architectural Books Available in America before the Revolution (1973)

graduation_rule.value: Ionic or Corinthian at the entrance and in the best room; Doric at the eave, porch and secondary doorway; Tuscan in service and dependency work

order.rule: One order governs the whole building and every moulding in it is derived from that order's module; where two orders are superimposed the heavier goes below.
order.note: The choice of Gibbs over Vignola or Palladio is evidentiary, not aesthetic: Gibbs's two books are among the most frequently recorded architectural titles in colonial American inventories, and the difference is measurable — 4.5 in of entablature on a 10 in column. Corinthian is listed but is rare and belongs only to the richest interiors and to a handful of porticos.

entasis.value: beginning at one third of the shaft height, not at the base

base.value: attic base: plinth, lower torus, scotia between fillets, upper torus

flutes.value: 24 in the Ionic where fluted; commonly plain in American work

column.rule: The column is nine diameters high, diminishes to 0.833 of its lower diameter with entasis beginning at a third of the shaft, and its plinth height is set by the order and not by the lumber yard.
column.note: American colonial columns are more often plain-shafted than fluted, which is a cost decision rather than a stylistic one and should not be read as a simplification of the order. The engine's Gibbs Ionic gives a full capital of one module against Vignola's 3 5/16 in at the same diameter — Gibbs draws a taller capital, and that is a real published difference and not an artefact.

internal_ratio.value: architrave = frieze, cornice = 4/3 of either (Gibbs invariant, engine-checked)

entablature.rule: The entablature is one fifth of the column, divided so that architrave and frieze are equal and the cornice is four thirds of either; it may be reduced by omitting enrichment but not by changing those ratios.
entablature.note: Both invariants here are checked by the proportion engine and hold. The one-fifth rule is Gibbs's and it is the reason to bind Gibbs at all: an American Georgian doorhead drawn to Vignola's quarter is 25 per cent too tall and looks it.

variants.note: Baroque furniture logic applied to a building. Broken and scrolled pediments are doorway forms only.
A scrolled pediment on a dormer is furniture logic at roof scale, and at that size the scrolls cannot be cut correctly in any case.

rise_over_span.note: at a 45 ft span; the ratio is 1:5

raking_cornice.value: the full cornice profile raked, with the corona level and the bed mould raked

tympanum.value: plain, or with a single oculus on the richest work

pediment.rule: A pediment's rise is one fifth of its span, its raking cornice carries the same profile as the level one, and a broken or scrolled pediment appears only over a doorway — never on a roof.
pediment.note: The doorway-only restriction on broken-scroll and swan-neck forms is a real period discipline and a common modern failure: a swan-neck pediment on a dormer or a portico is Baroque furniture logic applied to a building. The 1:5 figure from the facade pack sits inside the Palladian band, which is a small but genuine cross-check.

width_in.note: pilaster width where an order is applied to a bay or a pavilion, at a 9 ft bay

corner_pilaster_width_in.note: OQ 19: genuinely independent of the order, which is why it is editorial. The order decides a pilaster's width -- `width_in` above it is derived from the module -- and says nothing about a CORNER pilaster, which is a wider element answering two elevations at once and is a Georgian convention rather than a rule of the order.

capital.value: the same capital as the column of the bound order, in flat relief

diminution.value: pilasters diminish with the same 0.833 ratio as the columns they answer

pilaster.rule: A pilaster is the column of the bound order in flat relief, of the same height and diminution, projecting about a sixth of its width; it appears at the corners of the volume, flanking the entrance, and framing a centre pavilion.
pilaster.note: The pack figure (13.5 in at a 9 ft bay) and the measured New England corner pilaster (10-16 in) agree, which is worth noting because the same two sources disagree badly on the corner BOARD. The distinction the data cannot make is that a pilaster is an order and a corner board is a piece of trim; they land in different slots here only by accident of naming.

interior_dentil_height_in.note: OQ 19: independent of the order, and at a different scale from it. The order-derived members on this slot are the `modillion_*` parameters, which are exterior. An interior dentil is joinery run at room scale -- a chair rail's or a cornice's dentil course -- and no order states its size; that it appears on the same slot as the exterior modillion is the ontology grouping by element rather than by location.

interior_dentil_spacing_in.note: OQ 19: independent of the order, and at a different scale from it. The order-derived members on this slot are the `modillion_*` parameters, which are exterior. An interior dentil is joinery run at room scale -- a chair rail's or a cornice's dentil course -- and no order states its size; that it appears on the same slot as the exterior modillion is the ontology grouping by element rather than by location.

corner_rule.value: set out from the centre of the elevation; the corner member must be whole
corner_rule.note: A rule about SETTING OUT rather than dimension. 0.2.0 still has no type for this — it is a value of kind `measured` only because there is nothing better.

dentil_width_to_spacing.note: Each dentil about half its spacing wide, with twice its width between.

modillion_dentil.rule: Modillions or dentils are set out from the centre of the elevation so that the member at each corner is whole, and the two are not mixed on the same cornice except in the richest work where dentils sit below modillions.
modillion_dentil.note: The corner rule matters more than the spacing: a half dentil in a corner is the fastest way to spoil an otherwise good cornice, and it is what happens automatically when a cornice is ordered by the foot rather than set out. This is a rule about SETTING OUT rather than about dimension, and the parameters object has no way to express it — it survives only in the prose.

roof_deck_condition.value: only on a hipped roof with a flat deck, set back from the eave so it reads against the sky

balustrade.rule: A balustrade appears only on a hipped roof deck or a forecourt wall, is 30 to 33 in high with turned or square balusters at 4 to 6 in centres, and terminates in a pedestal at each end rather than in a post.

code_conflict.period_value: Balustrade height 30-33 in to the top of the rail
code_conflict.code_requirement: 36 in minimum guard height at a walking surface more than 30 in above grade
code_conflict.resolution: Keep the period height where the balustrade is decorative and unreachable — a roof deck with no occupiable access, or a forecourt wall below the 30 in trigger. Where the surface is occupiable, raise the whole assembly on a taller pedestal and plinth rather than stretching the baluster, which changes its proportion and is visible from the ground.

balustrade.note: The 30-33 in period height is below every modern guard code (36 in residential, 42 in commercial) and cannot be built as drawn on any accessible deck. The honest resolution is to keep the balustrade at period height where it is decorative and unreachable, and to add a concealed rail where it is not; the schema has no way to record a code override against a period dimension, which is a real gap for a buildable kit.

variants.note: Adamesque and Federal, from about 1785.
Adamesque low-relief ornament, from about 1785. Its shallowness is the point of it and it is the opposite of the bold cut relief this style is made of.
Pendant husk chains flanking a Federal mantel or doorway. Post-1785 and unmistakably not Georgian.
The Adam oval. Georgian ornament is square, round or acanthus; the oval is the Federal signature.
Low-relief Adamesque surface. This slot is where the Georgian/Federal boundary is most legible, and in 0.1.0 only half of it could be recorded.

relief.value: bold and deep, cut rather than applied; the relief is what separates Georgian from Federal more reliably than the motif does

concentration.value: the entrance, the chimney breast of the best room, and the stair; almost nothing elsewhere

ornament_vocabulary.rule: Ornament is carved in bold relief, belongs to the bound order, and is concentrated at the entrance and the chimney breast; it does not appear on the rear or the ends.
ornament_vocabulary.note: FORBIDDEN and unsayable: swag-and-urn, fan-and-patera, husk chains, oval paterae, reeding, and every other low-relief Adamesque motif — all of them Federal markers from about 1785. This slot is where the Georgian/Federal boundary is most legible and the schema forces the distinction into a note, because the permitted and forbidden vocabularies are both lists of variants and only one of them can be recorded.

variants.note: Victorian and later. Destroys the entrance as the single accented event.
Queen Anne.
A porch cut into the main volume is a Creole and Gulf Coast device.

two_tier_condition.value: only on the grandest houses, structurally integral with the wall, superimposed orders

porch_type.rule: The threshold is a raised stoop under a worked door surround; where a portico occurs it is one bay wide, centred, and carries the bound order.
porch_type.note: FORBIDDEN: full-width porch, wrap-around porch, and any porch that runs across more than the centre bay of a five-bay front — all of which are Victorian and later, and all of which destroy the reading of the entrance as the single accented event on an otherwise unaccented facade. Charleston is the standing exception and overrides this slot wholesale with the piazza, which is not a porch in this sense at all but an outdoor room on the flank.

porch_depth.rule: A Georgian entry portico is 5 to 8 ft deep — enough to stand out of the rain under, not enough to sit in; the depth is set by the projection of the order, not by use.
porch_depth.note: THE SLOT DEFINITION IS WRONG FOR THIS STYLE. The ontology's own note says 'below about 7 feet a porch is decoration; above it, it is a room. A hard constraint, not a preference.' That is a Craftsman and Queen Anne value judgment written into a universal slot. A Georgian entry portico is 5 to 6 ft deep and is SUPPOSED to be decoration; it is a piece of the order, not an outdoor room, and enlarging it to 7 ft to satisfy the slot's note would make it wrong. The slot note should be demoted from a constraint to an observation about porch-centred styles. STILL WRONG IN 0.2.0. The ontology note on this slot ('below about 7 feet a porch is decoration; above it, it is a room. A hard constraint, not a preference') is unchanged, and it remains a Craftsman value judgment sitting in a universal slot. Nothing in the kit schema can contradict a slot's own definition, which is correct — but the definition should be amended in elements/slots.json.

variants.note: Folk Victorian.
Vernacular and Gothic Revival.
Craftsman.
A 6x6 with a cap. No order, no diminution, no entasis.
Each free column must be answered by a pilaster on the wall behind. Without it the portico reads as furniture stood in front of the house.

engaged_pilaster.value: each free column answered by a pilaster on the wall behind it

spacing.value: set by the intercolumniation of the bound order, not by the width of the steps

porch_support.rule: Porch supports are columns of the bound order at full nine-diameter proportion, each answered by a pilaster on the wall behind, and spaced by the order's intercolumniation.
porch_support.note: FORBIDDEN: turned posts, chamfered posts, tapered battered piers on masonry bases, and dimensional lumber of any kind. The rule that each free column is answered by a pilaster is the one most often dropped and it is what makes a portico read as part of the wall rather than as furniture stood in front of it.

rail_profile.value: moulded handrail with a fillet and cyma, on a moulded shoe

porch_rail.rule: Where a rail is required the balusters are turned or square at 4 to 6 in centres between a moulded handrail and a moulded shoe, terminating in a newel or pedestal rather than in a post.

code_conflict.period_value: Rail height 30-33 in, balusters at 4-6 in centres
code_conflict.code_requirement: 36 in minimum guard height; 4 in maximum sphere between balusters
code_conflict.resolution: The baluster spacing conflict is resolved by taking the 4 in end of the period band, which is period-correct anyway. The height conflict is resolved by raising the whole assembly — a taller plinth under the balusters and a taller newel — rather than by lengthening the baluster, which changes its turned proportion. On a stoop of four or fewer risers no guard is required and the correct answer is no rail.

porch_rail.note: 'none' is the ordinary answer: a stoop of three or four risers has no rail in period work and needs none under code either. Where a rail is required by code the period height (30-33 in) is 3 in short of the 36 in minimum, and the honest answer is to raise the whole assembly rather than to stretch the balusters, which changes the proportion of the baluster and is visible. Again there is nowhere in the schema to record a code override against a period dimension.

porch_ceiling.note: STILL OPEN, AND 0.2.0 IMPROVED IT. The reason is now data rather than prose: determined_by records that the portico soffit is whatever the bound order's entablature requires, so the slot is not an independent variable. What remains unsaid is that the evidence is separately thin — few colonial porticos survive with original soffits — and that is what confidence: low is now carrying.

riser_height_in.note: two and a half courses, which is a good riser and NOT a whole number of courses — the honest problem in coursed step construction

platform_width_in.note: the entrance composition plus about 18 in of platform each side

material.value: stone or brick, laid solid; never a wood-framed deck

steps_and_stoop.rule: The stoop is a solid masonry platform, wider than the entrance composition by about 18 in each side, reached by three to five risers of 6 to 7 in with treads of 12 to 14 in.
steps_and_stoop.note: Deeper treads and lower risers than an interior stair, which is correct and is the opposite of what stock exterior step details do. The riser figure comes out of the brick module and lands at 6 7/8 in, which the pack itself flags as not being a whole number of courses — the mason has to fudge it, and period masons did.

set: the gate or the break in the fence line, on the entrance axis
the raised stoop platform, under the pediment of the door surround
the door itself, into the passage

through_view_required.note: Front and rear doors aligned on the passage axis, both real, both operable.

approach_geometry.value: frontal and axial; the house is met square-on, never obliquely

entry_sequence.rule: Three thresholds are crossed between the street and the hall — the gate on axis, the raised platform under the door surround, and the door — and at the moment the door opens the rear door on the same axis is visible through the passage.
entry_sequence.note: The through-view is the whole phenomenological argument of the style and it is a slot value, not a metaphor: front and rear doors aligned on the passage axis, both real, both operable, so the house can be seen straight through at the moment of entry. In the Chesapeake this is also a ventilation device and the child kit says so. This is the most consequential slot in the kit and it costs nothing to get right, which is why it is so often lost — the moment a coat closet or a powder room is put on the rear axis, the sequence collapses and no amount of correct trim recovers it.

from_storey_in.note: finished ceiling from storey height: subtract about 12 in for joist, subfloor, finish floor and ceiling

snapped_to_brick_course_in.note: in a brick building the storey height is not a free variable

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country

first_floor_low_country.note: Five feet taller than New England. Stack ventilation, not status.

ceiling_height_rule.rule: Ceilings of 9 to 11 ft on the principal floor and 8 to 10 ft above; in a masonry building the height is snapped to a whole number of brick courses before anything else is set out.

packs.note: Masonry only, and it runs first: in a brick building the storey height is not a free variable.

ceiling_height_rule.note: The regional band is one of the largest in the whole kit — a Charleston principal room is five feet taller than a New England one — and it is climatic rather than stylistic. It is also the parameter that most affects the interior trim, because trim-classical's nineteenth-part derivation is calibrated to rooms of 11 to 13 ft and misbehaves below about 9 ft 6 in.

variants.note: The successor style. Mixing families is the interior equivalent of mixing typefaces.
The successor's successor.
A different family entirely — flat stock, square edges, no order. Mixing it with classical profiles is the interior equivalent of mixing typefaces, which is the rule this slot exists to enforce.

wall_division.value: pedestal 4 : wall field 12 : entablature 3, in nineteen parts

full_entablature_height_in.note: where the room is to have a full entablature

picture_rail_bed_in.note: the line where the entablature begins; also the top of full-height panelling

cornice_member_count.note: Georgian 5: bed ovolo, dentils, corona, cyma, fillet. Federal 6, Greek Revival 4

grading_within_the_house.value: the best cornice in the parlour, a lesser one in the chamber, none in the garret

trim_family.rule: One profile family governs every internal moulding in the house — the Georgian section of trim-classical and no other — and the trim is graded down room by room by omitting members, never by changing family.

packs.note: In calibration for the entablature; see chair_rail for the member that is not.

trim_family.note: Grading trim by room is a real period habit and it is the thing that makes an eighteenth-century house feel hierarchical rather than uniform. It is also almost impossible to record in this schema: the kit has one value per slot per style, and 'the parlour cornice has five members and the chamber cornice three' needs a per-room dimension the ontology does not have. The plan-logic group anticipates a room catalogue; this is the slot that will most need it.

height_in.note: Georgian family multiplier 1.00; Federal 0.85, Greek Revival 1.27

height_alt_in.note: the same member taken from the storey

thickness_in.note: 4/4 stock dressed, not the 1/2 in of modern primed base

profile.value: square plinth board with a cyma reversa cap and fillet

baseboard.rule: The base is a real plinth — a square board 8 to 9 in high at a 9 ft ceiling, capped with a cyma reversa — and it must be thicker than the casing that dies into it.
baseboard.note: The base-thicker-than-casing relationship is the reason the plinth block exists, and it is the single most reliable structural test of whether a trim package was designed or assembled: if the casing is thicker than the base, the base has to be scribed to the casing and the joint opens with the first heating season.

width_in.note: one sixth of the void; the modern default is one sixteenth

plinth_block_height_in.note: one inch above the top of the base

window_casing_width_in.note: wider than the door casing in the same room

doorhead_over_interior_door_in.note: full entablature over an interior door in a principal room

profile.value: two or three fasciae with an astragal between and a cyma reversa cap, with a backband

casing.rule: Casing width is one sixth of the opening it trims — 6 in on a 36 in door — with a backband projecting about 1 in, dying into a plinth block 1 in taller than the base.

packs.note: The most useful rule in the pack: exactly stated in a primary source, dimensionless, and almost universally got wrong.

casing.note: Named by the pack as the single most useful rule it carries, because it is exactly stated in a primary source, dimensionless, and almost universally got wrong. The window casing being wider than the door casing in the same room is the counter-intuitive part and it is well attested.

height_in.note: where only a cornice is run, which is the ordinary case

projection_in.note: projection onto the ceiling equal to its height on the wall — a 45 degree cornice

crown.rule: A crown of about 7 in at a 9 ft ceiling, projecting as far onto the ceiling as it stands on the wall; in a principal room the crown is replaced by the full entablature at three nineteenths of the wall.

packs.note: Gives the PROJECTION, not the height. The packs reuse slot names for different members and this is the clearest case.

crown.note: The 45 degree cornice is the classical default and the modern stock crown projects about half its height, which is why it reads as a strip rather than as a member. The three packs bound here give 6.8 in, 8.6 in and 4.5 in for related but not identical members, and disentangling which is the crown, which is the whole cornice and which is the projection took longer than it should have — the packs use the same slot name for different members.

profile.value: astragal, cyma reversa, corona and listel — the corona is the member a chair back actually hits

height.note: The operative figure. Same datum as the window sill, which is not a coincidence.

from_wall_division.note: The pure nineteenth-part derivation. Out of calibration below an 11 ft ceiling — see packs.

chair_rail.rule: The chair rail sits at 30 to 32 in above the finished floor, on the same datum as the window sill, and its corona must project further than the base cap or it will not shed a chair.

packs.note: 30.7 in at a 9 ft ceiling. Agrees with the measured band.
32.4 in. Also agrees.

22.7 in at a 9 ft ceiling, ten inches below the other two. NOT NOISE: the pedestal derivation was calibrated for rooms of 11-13 ft and the pack says so itself; below that it puts the rail under the back of a chair. in_calibration false is exactly the field this needed. NOTE THE FLAG IS STATIC AND THE CONDITION IS NOT: the derivation reaches the measured 30 in band only at a 142.5 in ceiling, so it stays false through the whole New England and Chesapeake range and becomes true only in Charleston. A boolean cannot express that; what the field wants is the ceiling range over which it holds.

chair_rail.note: THE CLEAREST CASE IN THIS EXERCISE OF TWO BOUND PACKS CONTRADICTING EACH OTHER. At a 9 ft ceiling trim-classical's derivation gives 22.7 in, storey-graduation gives 30.7 in and gibbs-ionic gives 32.4 in. The 10 in spread is not noise: trim-classical's pedestal rule was calibrated for rooms of 11-13 ft and it says so, and below that it puts the rail under the back of a chair. Two packs against one, plus the measured evidence, so the rule is set at 30-32 in and the pure derivation is recorded as a parameter rather than as the answer. NOTHING IN THE SCHEMA ARBITRATES THIS. A style binds N packs, several of them speak to the same slot, and there is no precedence field, no conflict record, and no way for the resolver to know that one of the three is out of its calibrated range.

panel_field_height_in.note: the clear panel between base cap and surbase

panel_width_in.note: dado panels run WIDER than tall, typically 1.5 to 1.8 to 1

full_height_panelling.value: the chimney wall of the best room only; the other three walls plastered above the dado

wainscot.rule: The dado is raised and fielded panelling whose panels run wider than tall at 1.5 to 1.8 to 1, set out from the centre of the wall or the centre of the chimney breast so that no panel is a fragment and the panels flanking an opening are equal.

packs.note: Below 9 in of clear field, abandon the dado for plaster and a rail.

wainscot.note: The asymmetry between the chimney wall and the other three is the most characteristic thing about a Georgian room and it is not a cost compromise — the panelled chimney breast is the most expensive object in the house and the plaster around it is what makes it read. Below 9 in of clear panel field the dado should be abandoned for plaster and a rail; at an 8 ft ceiling the derivation produces a slot rather than a panel.

height_in.note: a door should occupy about seven tenths of the wall

height_alt_in.note: Palladio's maximum room door, within half an inch of the modern 6 ft 8 in stock door

graduation.value: principal rooms six-panel, chambers six or four, service two-panel or batten

interior_door.rule: Interior doors are six-panel raised and fielded in principal rooms, sized so that the leaf is about 0.7 of the ceiling height, and graduated down to four panels and then to batten as the rooms lose rank.

packs.note: Palladio's maximum room door, within half an inch of the modern 6 ft 8 in stock door.

interior_door.note: The convergence of Palladio's maximum room door with the modern 6 ft 8 in stock door is genuine and worth knowing when someone claims the stock door is an unhistorical imposition. What IS modern is the refusal to go above it: at an 11 ft ceiling the rule wants a 92 in door and a 6 ft 8 in one occupies 61 per cent of the wall and reads as a hatch.

landing_position.value: the stair rises in the passage against one side wall and turns at a landing lit by a window on the rear or side elevation

riser_height.note: Conventional field-measurement band for eighteenth-century principal stairs. I could not verify a specific documented figure in the available sources and 0.2.0's `kind` field is where that admission now lives — this is editorial, not measured.

stair_type.rule: The principal stair rises in the passage in two or three runs against one side wall, open-string with carved and applied bracket ends on the best work, turning at a landing that is lit by its own window.

code_conflict.code_requirement: Riser 7.75 in maximum, tread 10 in minimum
code_conflict.resolution: A period-correct principal stair is not buildable as drawn. Taking the shallow end of the period band (7.75 in riser, 10 in tread) is legal and is inside the historical range, but it adds a riser per storey and lengthens the run by about 10 in, which eats the passage the plan is organised around. Where the passage cannot absorb it, add a winder-free landing and turn the stair earlier rather than reducing the passage width below the 10 ft minimum.

stair_type.note: RISER AND TREAD ARE A HONEST WEAK POINT. The 7.5-8.5 in riser and 9-10.5 in tread band is the conventional field-measurement range for eighteenth-century principal stairs and I could not verify a specific documented figure in the sources available; treat it as an editorial band rather than a measured one. It also conflicts with the IRC directly — 7.75 in max riser and 10 in min tread — so a period-correct stair is not buildable as drawn, and the resolution (a shallower stair with more risers, which lengthens the run and eats the passage) is a real design consequence that the kit should carry and cannot.

baluster_pattern.value: where three per tread, commonly twisted, fluted and plain in rotation

handrail.value: moulded, ramped and eased into the newel rather than butted to it

step_end_brackets.value: carved and applied to the open string, one per tread

newel_balustrade.rule: Three balusters to a tread in the best work and two in ordinary work, carrying a moulded handrail that ramps and eases into a turned column newel; the open string carries a carved bracket at each tread end.

code_conflict.period_value: Handrail 30-32 in above the tread nosing
code_conflict.resolution: Set the rail at 34 in — the code minimum and only 2 in above the period band, which is within the tolerance of the ramp-and-ease anyway. Do not stretch the balusters: lengthen the newel and re-cut the ramp, which is where the 2 in should be absorbed.

newel_balustrade.note: The ramp-and-ease is what separates a joiner's stair from a carpenter's and it is the most expensive 18 inches in the house. Same code conflict as the porch rail: the period handrail sits 2 to 4 in below the modern minimum.

variants.note: The earlier form, largely gone by 1760.
The best room only.
Applied gesso swags and urns. Post-1785.

shelf_height_in.note: marked judgment; the measured Georgian band is 42-56 in

overmantel.value: panelled to the cornice on the chimney wall of the best room

hearth.value: stone or brick, projecting 18-24 in into the room

fireplace_surround.rule: The fireplace is the accented wall of the room: a bolection or full architrave surround with a shelf at 42 to 56 in, and in the best room a panelled overmantel carried to the cornice.

packs.note: Judgment-marked in the pack; the measured 42-56 in band is the operative figure and this is the check.

fireplace_surround.note: The bolection surround is the earlier form and is largely gone by 1760; the pilastered and shelved form is what most people picture. The shelf-height rule is marked judgment in the pack and the reason is good — the height is set as much by the firebox and the overmantel as by the wall — so the measured band is the operative figure and the derivation is a check.

corner_cupboard_shell_radius.value: the shell head is a half dome, its radius half the cupboard width

window_seat_condition.value: masonry walls only, where the reveal is 4-8 in and the wall is 13.5 in or more

built_ins.rule: Built-ins are architectural rather than joinery afterthoughts: a shell-top corner cupboard in the best room, closets flanking the chimney breast where the stack allows, and window seats only where the wall is thick enough to make one.
built_ins.note: THE HONEST PROBLEM IN THIS SLOT IS ABSENCE. The Georgian house has almost no storage — the style node names 'a plan without closets, bathrooms or a garage' as a diagnostic against Colonial Revival — and a buildable modern kit needs closets in every bedroom, which the plan has nowhere to put without either thickening the walls or eating the room. That is a real and unsolved conflict between the historical kit and the buildable one, and it belongs in the same category as garage_strategy: a place where the kit must author rather than retrieve. I have not authored it here because, unlike the garage, it has no single defensible answer — it is a plan problem, not an elevation problem, and it should be solved in the room catalogue when that exists. 0.2.0 splits the closet out to storage_strategy, which is where the unsolved half of this note now lives. What remains here is genuine joinery and is well documented.

variants.note: Post-dates the style by a century and a half and is the commonest single anachronism in a restored colonial interior.
A floor of uniform 8 in boards is as wrong as strip oak, differently. Random width is the operative word.
The bevel casts a line at every board edge that a face-nailed plank floor does not have.

plank_laying.value: random width, running the long dimension of the room, face-nailed with cut or rose-head nails

brick_paving_location.value: passage, cellar, kitchen and dependency floors

floor_material.rule: Floors are random-width softwood or oak plank of 6 to 14 in, laid the long way of the room and face-nailed; masonry paving is used in the passage and in service spaces.
floor_material.note: FORBIDDEN in effect: 2 1/4 in strip oak, which post-dates the style by a century and a half and is the commonest single anachronism in a restored colonial interior. Random width is the important word — a floor of uniform 8 in boards is as wrong as a floor of 2 1/4 in strip, differently.

variants.note: Batten and service doors.
Principal rooms.
Arrives about 1775. A hard boundary: butt hinges on a house dated 1740 are wrong in a way a specialist sees immediately.

A lever handle has no eighteenth-century existence and the escutcheon plate is the wrong shape for a period door stile. Where accessibility requires a lever, use a period-profile lever on a plain rose and say plainly that it is a substitution.
A cup hinge on a period cupboard door. The whole point of colonial hardware is that it is visible and wrought.

finish.value: wrought and blackened iron in ordinary rooms; brass box locks and knobs in principal rooms

shutter_hardware.value: pintles set into the jamb, with a shutter dog at each leaf

hardware.rule: Hinges are surface-mounted wrought iron before about 1775 and the door hardware is graded with the room — brass box locks in the principal rooms, iron thumb latches everywhere else.
hardware.note: The 1775 date for cast butt hinges is the most useful single fact in this slot because it is a hard boundary: a house presented as 1740 with butt hinges is wrong in a way a specialist will see immediately and nobody else will. Hardware is also the one slot where correct reproductions are cheap and readily available, which makes getting it wrong unforced.

light_fixture_family.note: LEFT OPEN, AND THE REASON IS NOT LACK OF EVIDENCE. What the historical style has is well known and thin: candle sconces on the panelling, a hanging candle lantern in the passage, and a chandelier in the very best rooms — plus the fact that most eighteenth-century lighting was PORTABLE and therefore not architecture at all. The reason to leave it open rather than to specify a modern equivalent is that, unlike garage_strategy, nothing in the building depends on the answer: a wrong fixture is swapped out in an afternoon and changes no other slot. Authoring an invention here would be gold-plating an ontology slot that carries no consequences, and it would obscure the two places where invention genuinely is required.

variants.note: The First Period plan, and the thing the Georgian plan was invented to replace.
No eighteenth-century existence at all.
The vernacular predecessor. Two rooms, no passage, one entered through the other.
English medieval.

passage_share_of_facade.value: roughly one third on a five-bay front; one fifth to one quarter on a seven-bay

passage_runs.value: front to back, full depth, with an exterior door at each end

side_hall_condition.value: urban lots only, three bays wide

circulation_parti.rule: A passage 10 to 14 ft wide runs the full depth of the house from front door to rear door, dividing it into two equal halves, with every principal room opening off it and no room entered through another.
circulation_parti.note: FORBIDDEN: the central-chimney lobby entrance, which is the First Period plan and the thing the Georgian plan was invented to replace, and the open plan, which has no eighteenth-century existence at all. The passage is the style's central social invention — it is what makes privacy possible — and it is not a corridor: at 10 to 14 ft it is wider than most modern bedrooms and it was furnished and used as a room.

variants.note: First Period. The single fastest discriminator.
Dutch and French colonial.

position_new_england.value: interior, 5-12 ft in from the gable ends, flanking the ridge

position_mid_atlantic.value: at or within the gable ends

position_tidewater.value: gable ends, interior-end or fully exterior

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country

breast_position_in_room.value: on the outside wall of the room, opposite or beside the passage door
breast_position_in_room.note: Moved here from `room_adjacency_overrides` on 24 Aug 2026 (OQ 15). It was one of six clauses in that slot's flat prose set and it is not an adjacency rule at all -- it says where a physical element sits within a room, which is what this slot is for. The regional `position_*` parameters beside it say where the STACK goes in the building; this says where the breast lands in the room, which is a different question with a different answer and they are both needed to draw the room.

hearth_position.rule: Hearths are paired and symmetrical about the passage axis, never a single central stack, and their position on the gable-to-ridge axis is a climate decision that each region settles differently.
hearth_position.note: This is the fossil of the heating strategy and the fastest regional discriminator in the style. The New England answer keeps the stack's stored heat inside the envelope; the Southern answer pushes it outside. Both are correct and they are opposite, which is exactly the sort of thing the cascade handles well: the parent states the invariant (paired, symmetrical, never central) and each child states its own resolution of the free axis.

landing_window.value: required, on the rear or side elevation

service_stair.value: a second, narrower, enclosed stair serving the service end where the house has one

stair_position.rule: The principal stair stands in the passage against one side wall, starting far enough back from the front door that the passage reads as a room before it reads as a stair, and it turns at a landing lit by its own window.
stair_position.note: The setback is the whole trick and it is the difference between a hall and a stairwell. A stair that starts at the front door turns the passage into circulation; a stair that starts 8 ft back leaves a square room at the front of the house that happens to have a stair at the end of it. The landing window is a genuine constraint that fights the facade rule — it must land between the storey head datums and so it either breaks the one-datum rule or it lights the landing badly, and period houses cheat this constantly.

set: front rooms: formal, entered by invitation
service and dependency: separate circulation entirely

gradient_axis.value: front to back and ground to first, both at once

public_private_gradient.rule: Rank falls front to back and rises then falls ground to attic; no room is entered through another, and the service circulation never crosses the formal one except at the passage.
public_private_gradient.note: This is the slot that carries the style's actual social content, which the style node states plainly: the Georgian house is a machine for making a stratifying society legible and liveable, and it separates the family from the servants and enslaved workers who ran it. Recording the gradient without recording what produced it would make the kit a costume. The one thing the modern kit cannot inherit is the separate service circulation, because there is no longer a service class to circulate — which means the rear stair and the back passage have to be re-justified on other grounds or dropped.

room_adjacency_overrides.rule: Every principal room opens off the passage and nothing else; doors align across the passage on a common axis; no room is a route to another.
room_adjacency_overrides.note: OQ 15, CLOSED 24 Aug 2026. This slot held six rules of four different kinds as a flat set of prose strings in one 'many'-cardinality parameter -- a topological rule about the adjacency graph, a geometric rule about axes, a rule about where a wall element goes, and a preference about orientation. They are not the same species and no engine could act on them as written. Resolved: TWO were about the adjacency graph and are now typed `rules` above (the second of them folding in a clause that restated it). THREE were duplication of slots that already say the same thing, and are deleted rather than moved -- 'the best room is at the front, on the side away from the service end' is `public_private_gradient`'s own rule sentence ('Rank falls front to back'); 'no principal room is a through-route to another' is that same slot's 'no room is entered through another' and this slot's own first clause; 'windows on two walls of every principal room' is `daylight_strategy`'s `walls_lit_per_principal_room: 2` and its rule sentence verbatim. ONE was not about adjacency at all -- the chimney breast's position within the room -- and has moved to `hearth_position`, which owns where the hearth goes. A style that states a universal rule here is duplicating data that will drift; that was true of half of what was here.

rules.statement: Every principal room opens directly off the passage and off nothing else, so no principal room is a route to another.
rules.why: This is what a centre passage IS, and what distinguishes the Georgian plan from the hall-and-parlor it replaced: the passage takes the through traffic so the rooms stop being corridors. The universal room records do not forbid a door between two principal rooms -- an enfilade is a legitimate arrangement elsewhere -- so this narrows them.
rules.note: Folded in the sixth clause of the old flat set, 'no principal room is a through-route to another principal room', which stated the same restriction a second time (OQ 15).

rules.statement: Doors across the passage align on a common axis, so the enfilade reads through the house from front door to rear.
rules.why: A requirement no room record makes, and one of the two or three things that most reliably separates a designed Georgian plan from a room list with a corridor. The tolerance is the `door_alignment_tolerance` parameter beside this: zero inches.

strategy_low_country.value: detached in the rear yard, linked by a covered way, plus a basement service floor

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country

service_zone_strategy.rule: Service is removed from the main block — detached, hyphenated or in the basement — and it has its own circulation which does not cross the formal plan except at the passage.
service_zone_strategy.note: The detachment was fire control and heat control before it was social, and in the South it was both. The modern kit inherits the FORM of this rule with none of its content: nobody will put a kitchen 25 ft away from the house, so the detached dependency becomes a garage, a guest suite or a pool house, and the kitchen comes into the rear of the main block where the style has no vocabulary for it. That substitution is defensible but it is a substitution and should be recorded as one. Reconciled 23 Aug 2026 (docs/open-questions.md #17, docs/inheritance.md): the strategy_tidewater applies_when.regions parameter that duplicated tidewater-georgian is removed from here -- that variant node exists precisely because Tidewater diverges enough to deserve its own identity (massing, exemplars, name), so its own kit binding is now the sole statement of the fact, not a second mechanism restating what the variant already states. strategy_new_england/strategy_mid_atlantic/strategy_low_country are unaffected: none of their corresponding variant nodes currently binds this slot, so applies_when.regions remains the correct mechanism for those three, per the same ruling.

frame_bay_ft.note: the 16 ft timber bay is why a frame double-pile lands at 32-38 ft and not 40

depth_and_pile.rule: Double-pile at 32 to 40 ft deep is the Northern and Mid-Atlantic norm; single-pile at 18 to 22 ft is the Chesapeake answer and it is a ventilation decision, not a poverty one.
depth_and_pile.note: The single-pile Chesapeake house is the clearest case in the style of a plan decision driven entirely by climate: one room deep means every room has windows on two opposite walls and the whole house cross-ventilates. It survived in Virginia for decades after New England went double-pile, and the reason is summer, not money.

glazing_ratio_of_floor_area.note: the glazing ratio is the honest measure of how rich the building is, and it moved with the price of glass

passage_lit.value: at both ends, through the front and rear doors and their transoms

daylight_strategy.rule: Every principal room is lit from two walls, the passage is lit at both ends, and the total glazing runs around a tenth of the floor area — which is dark by modern standards and is what the rooms were designed for.

packs.note: Glazing as a fraction of floor area. Dark by modern standards and what the rooms were designed for.
Window area to wall area on the front. Different quantity.

daylight_strategy.note: The tenth-of-floor-area figure is worth stating because it is the number a modern client will refuse. A Georgian room at 10 per cent glazing is genuinely dim, the deep reveals and the light-coloured panelling are compensations for it, and doubling the glazing to modern expectations changes the pier-to-void ratio on the facade and therefore breaks window_grouping_rule. That is a real cascade of consequences from one comfort decision and the schema records none of it.

variants.note: The period answer where there is one: the residual space beside a gable-end stack, 18-30 in deep, with a panelled door in the same family as the room.
Under the service stair and on its landings.
The attic is the house's storage and always was.

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country

variants.note: Detached: the dairy, the smokehouse, the office. Removing storage from the main block is the period habit and it is the one worth borrowing.
A small room rather than a closet, entered from one chamber. Documented in the largest houses and the most defensible way to get modern closet volume without a closet.
A recess formed in the thickness of a masonry wall, which is where a window seat also comes from.
AUTHORED, and the honest compromise. It works only if it is taken out of the depth of the plan and not out of the width, because the width is set by the bay rhythm and the depth is not.
It blinds a bay. A closet placed against the outside wall either eliminates a window or leaves a window inside a closet, and both are visible from the street.
The commonest way a modern plan destroys entry_sequence: a coat closet or a powder room placed on the rear axis kills the through-view and no amount of correct trim recovers it.

permitted_wall_for_closets.value: interior partitions and the chimney wall only

rear_axis_keep_clear.note: No storage may occupy the rear passage axis. This is a hard rule and it is the whole reason the slot exists.

closet_depth_min.note: Below 24 in a hanging closet does not work, which is the constraint that makes this a plan problem rather than a joinery one.

storage_strategy.rule: Storage is taken out of the depth of the plan, never out of the bay rhythm: closets go against interior partitions and the chimney wall, the garret and the dependencies carry the bulk, and nothing is placed on the rear passage axis.
storage_strategy.note: AUTHORED, and it is the second of the two genuinely invented slots. In the last report I declined to author it because it had no single defensible answer; having a slot of its own changes that, because the answer no longer has to pretend to be joinery. What is retrieved: the chimney-flanking closet, the garret, the dependency, the dressing room and the masonry recess are all period. What is invented: the rule that closets may only occupy interior partitions and the chimney wall, and the absolute prohibition on the rear axis. The second of those I would defend as hard as the garage rule — it protects the one slot in the kit that costs nothing and is most often destroyed.

variants.note: AUTHORED FROM THE PLAN'S OWN LOGIC. The gable-end stack is already a vertical mass running the full height of the house with no windows in it; plumbing stacks, flues and duct risers go beside it, inside the same chase. It is the only place in a Georgian plan where a vertical service run costs nothing.
Equipment in the subordinate volume the style already has, which is where the kitchen was for the same reasons of noise and fire.
Distribution in the floor structure between joists, running parallel to the joists and not across them, which the 16 ft timber bay makes possible.
Wholly detached, in the dependency the style already uses for the noisy and the dangerous. The best answer where the composition is five-part.
The passage is a room with a full cornice. A duct soffit running its length turns the style's central social invention into a corridor.
A condensing unit inside the approach cone, at the base of the wall the composition is about. It belongs behind the front plane and screened, which the parameters state.
Already stated at roof_penetration_rules; repeated here because it is a services decision made by a mechanical contractor who will never read that slot.
Any horizontal run that has to cross the centre passage forces either a dropped soffit or a raised floor, and both break the section.

chase_width_beside_stack.note: Enough for a 4 in stack, a flue liner and a small riser. Asserted from the plumbing, not from the fabric.

equipment_location.value: service ell, basement or detached dependency

condenser_position.value: behind the front plane of the main block, screened by a wall or hedge

duct_direction_rule.value: parallel to the joists, in the bay, never perpendicular
duct_direction_rule.note: Follows from the timber-bay pack: the 16 ft bay gives a clear run in one direction only.

services_strategy.rule: Vertical services run in a chase beside the chimney mass, equipment lives in the service ell or the dependency, horizontal distribution runs parallel to the joists within a bay, and nothing crosses the centre passage.

packs.note: The bay is what makes a parallel-to-joist duct run possible at all.

services_strategy.note: WHOLLY AUTHORED — there is no eighteenth-century content here whatever, and the confidence is low because this is a first draft of something that ought to be argued about with a mechanical engineer rather than written by me. What makes it defensible rather than arbitrary is that every rule is derived from a slot the style already has: the chimney mass is already a full-height blind vertical, the service ell is already where the noisy and dangerous things went, and the timber bay already gives a clear joist run in one direction. The single most valuable line is the prohibition on crossing the passage, because that is the decision that quietly destroys the plan and it is made late, by someone else, on a different drawing.

approach.value: on the entrance axis, so the front is met square-on

two_front_condition.value: plantation houses with a land front and a river front, both fully composed

urban_condition.value: the front wall on the street line, entrance directly on the pavement with a stoop of 3-5 risers

street_relationship.rule: The house presents a composed front square-on to its approach, and where it has two approaches it has two fully composed fronts; it is never seen obliquely as a picturesque object.
street_relationship.note: The two-front condition is a genuinely different building from the one-front condition and it is much more expensive, because the composition rules apply twice with no cheating on the back. Westover and the great James River houses are the case, and it is one of the few places in American building where the rear elevation is as good as the front.

setback_rule.note: LEFT OPEN DELIBERATELY, AND THIS IS THE CLEANEST 'OPEN' IN THE KIT. The style genuinely does not fix a setback: the same grammar, the same trim, the same plan is built on the street line in Annapolis and Philadelphia and at the end of a half-mile approach at Westover. The variation is a settlement-pattern variable and not a style variable, and inventing a number here would be putting a suburban front-yard convention into a taxon that predates the front yard. What CAN be said is said in street_relationship and grade_relationship; this slot should stay open at the style level and be specified by the site, or at most by the massing. 0.2.0 does not change this and should not: it is genuinely a settlement variable, not a style variable, and open is the correct binding.

governing_factor.value: the approach and the composition, not the sun

chimney_axis.value: the ridge runs across the approach axis so the chimneys are seen against the sky from the front

passage_axis.value: front to back on the approach axis, which sets the cross-ventilation axis whether or not it suits the prevailing wind

orientation_rule.rule: The house is oriented to its approach and to symmetry; the entrance faces the road or the water and everything else follows from that.
orientation_rule.note: A REAL LIABILITY, STATED PLAINLY. Georgian orientation logic is indifferent to the sun, which means that a correctly oriented Georgian house can face north with its principal rooms in permanent shade, and there is no rule in the style to prevent it. Charleston is the exception that proves it: the piazza must face within 45 degrees of southwest, and that is the one place the tradition put climate ahead of the approach. Any modern application of this style has to decide whether to inherit the indifference or to override it, and the schema gives no way to flag a slot as 'inherited but deprecated'. The 'inherited but deprecated' flag I asked for is still absent in 0.2.0. There is no way to mark a rule as correct-for-the-period and dangerous-to-inherit, which is exactly what this slot is.

arrangement.value: symmetrically disposed about the entrance axis where they are visible from the approach; informally grouped in the service yard where they are not

outbuilding_types.rule: Outbuildings that are visible from the approach are composed symmetrically about the axis and subordinated in height; outbuildings in the service yard are not composed at all.
outbuilding_types.note: The quarters are named explicitly and should stay named. A Chesapeake or Low Country Georgian plantation complex is a machine run by enslaved labour, the dependencies are where that labour lived and worked, and a kit that lists the dovecote and omits the quarters is not being tactful, it is being false. The formal-versus-informal split is real and is worth keeping: the same complex is a composition on the approach side and a working yard behind.

picket_spacing.value: picket width to picket gap roughly 1:1

wall_coping.value: moulded or bevelled brick, or stone

fence_wall.rule: The forecourt is enclosed by a painted picket fence or a brick wall with piers, with the gate on the entrance axis; field boundaries are post-and-rail.
fence_wall.note: The forecourt enclosure is the first of the three thresholds in entry_sequence and it is the one most often omitted in modern work, which is why so many otherwise correct houses feel as though they are standing in a field. The ha-ha is included because it belongs to the same period landscape logic — a boundary that does not interrupt the view — and it is the one landscape device in the list that a modern site can still use.

variants.note: Arrives in America after 1780. The site-scale equivalent of the ornament_vocabulary boundary and it dates just as precisely.
Shrubs banked against the wall. A twentieth-century habit that buries the water table, which is the datum the whole elevation is measured from.
An unenclosed lawn removes the first of the three thresholds and is why so many otherwise correct houses feel as though they are standing in a field.

geometry.value: rectilinear, axial, symmetrical about the entrance axis

planting.value: clipped and architectural near the house; the picturesque begins beyond the ha-ha if at all

terrace_falls.value: the falls at Middleton Place and the Chesapeake terraced gardens are the canonical case

landscape_idiom.rule: The landscape near the house is geometric and axial — forecourt, terraces, allee, walled garden in quarters — and it is composed with the elevation rather than around it.
landscape_idiom.note: FORBIDDEN and unsayable again: the picturesque, serpentine, informally massed landscape, which arrives in America after 1780 and is a Federal and Romantic idiom. This is the site-scale equivalent of the ornament_vocabulary boundary and it dates just as precisely. Foundation planting in the modern sense — shrubs banked against the wall to hide the foundation — is a twentieth-century habit and it destroys the water table, which is the datum the whole elevation is measured from.

grade_fall_away_from_wall.value: not less than 6 in in the first 10 ft

raised_basement_condition.value: Charleston and urban Mid-Atlantic; the principal floor a full storey above grade with the entry stair rising to it

grade_relationship.rule: The house sits on a plinth: the water table stands 24 to 36 in above finished grade on every elevation, and the grade falls away from the wall rather than being banked against it.
grade_relationship.note: The 'on every elevation' clause is the hard part on a sloping site and it is why period houses on falling ground get a fully exposed basement on the low side rather than a water table that wanders. A water table that follows the grade is the tell that the house was drawn in elevation and not in section.
